prs.title: [ci] Fix test axis fixtures never running their off state in CI
prs.author: unstubbable
prs.body:
Fixtures can key an experimental flag on `__NEXT_TEST_AXIS`, so that the Cache Components run covers the off state of that flag. Only `scripts/run-jest.sh` derived the axis from `__NEXT_CACHE_COMPONENTS`. CI starts Jest through `run-tests.js`, which does not run that script. The Cache Components jobs therefore ran these fixtures with the flag on, the same as the plain jobs.

The alias now lives in a Jest `globalSetup` file, which `run-jest.sh` and `run-tests.js` both load through `jest.config.js`. Jest runs it in its main process before it starts any workers, so test files and the processes they start inherit the value. A per-test setup file would only change the copy of `process.env` that Jest gives each test file.

Deploy tests had a second gap. Vercel environment variable names cannot start with an underscore, so the harness writes forwarded flags into the deployed `next.config` as assignments. `__NEXT_TEST_AXIS` was not one of these flags. The harness also added the assignments after the config content, which is too late for a flag that the config reads while it loads. The harness now forwards the axis and inserts the assignments first.

This also changes what two fixtures see on deploy. `optimistic-route-cache-keying-regression` and `sub-shell-generation-middleware` read `__NEXT_CACHE_COMPONENTS` while their config loads, so the Cache Components deploy run now enables `partialPrefetching` for them, as their configs intend.

prs.title: Stop patching error inspection if source maps are disabled
prs.author: eps1lon
prs.body:
If source maps are disabled, we're most likely running in a prod server where sourcemapping happens lazily when logs are inspected. Ignore-listing generated frames would forever hide n_m frames.

It also avoids doing a bunch of work that just won't have any effect.

As a follow-up, I'll experiment with showing all frames during next-build if all original frames are ignore-listed since that's a one-shot process. For next-dev, we'll continue showing no frames if everything is ignore-listed since you have an attached a debugger with the browser to get a high-fidelity UI to see ignore-listed frames.

prs.title: Turbopack: store ChunkGroupInfo::chunk_groups as a Vec
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
Order matters, use a vec

Using IndexSet gives us 'set equality' semantics (but deterministic iteration order),  this is broken for chunk groups and can cause queries that depend on ordering to fail.  Since in a wam build if the order of items in a chunk group changes, then we will reuse the old order (the cell update is considered equivalent)

I am looking at other places where this is a risk but this one definitely is and is straightforward to fix

prs.title: fix(turbopack): avoid panics from transient chunk group indices
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

In `next dev` with Turbopack lazy dynamic imports (`experimental.turbopackLazyDynamicImports` and/or `turbopackLazyDynamicImportsSSR`), apps with nested `React.lazy(() => import(...))` client components log Rust panics while lazy imports activate:

```
thread 'tokio-rt-worker' panicked at turbopack/crates/turbopack-core/src/module_graph/chunk_group_info.rs:111:51:
index out of bounds: the len is 31 but the index is 31
```

The dev server recovers and pages render, but the output is noisy and the panics hide real errors. This PR turns that out-of-range lookup into a contextual, transient error and adds regression coverage. It doesn't touch #100705 or canonicalization (#100705 was reverted in #100898). The panic happens on canary without it.

### Why?

`compute_chunk_group_info` creates the `module_chunk_groups` and `chunk_group_indices` child cells with `ResolvedVc::cell(...)` while it builds the result, and creates the outer `ChunkGroupInfo` cell, which holds `chunk_groups` inline, at the end. Each cell is published when it is written (`turbo-tasks-backend/src/backend/operation/update_cell.rs`). So while lazy activation recomputes the graph, an eventually consistent reader of `get_chunk_groups_for_module` (or `get_chunk_group`) can pair the **old** inline `chunk_groups` with a **new** child cell. If the new graph has more chunk groups, `self.chunk_groups[index]` is out of range.

prs.title: fix(turbopack): fix canary build after chunk_groups became a Vec
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
### What?

Fixes the canary build. `turbopack-core` doesn't compile since #100928 merged:

```
error[E0599]: no method named `get_index` found for struct `Vec<ChunkGroup>` in the current scope
```

### Why?

This is a semantic merge conflict:

- #100935 changed `ChunkGroupInfo::chunk_groups` from an `FxIndexSet<ChunkGroup>` to a `Vec<ChunkGroup>`.
- #100928's `ChunkGroupInfo::chunk_group_at` was tested on a base without that change. It still calls `get_index`, which exists only on `IndexSet`.

### How?

Use `Vec::get`. It returns the same `Option<&ChunkGroup>`, so the error context and behavior stay the same. No other code has `IndexSet`-only calls on `chunk_groups`.

Verified locally with `cargo fmt --check` and with `cargo check -p turbopack-core --all-targets` under `-D warnings`.

prs.title: Fix prerendering of caught `'use cache'` errors
prs.author: unstubbable
prs.body:
The error handler records errors thrown inside `'use cache'` functions in the work store's digest lookup. The page renderer uses that lookup to recover original errors for logging (#86500). Prerendering also uses it to detect render failures, so errors caught by the page can still fail the build or on-demand generation.

This change collects errors reported by the page's RSC renderer separately and preserves the shared lookup for logging. The regression covers caught errors from `'use cache'` functions during build-time and on-demand prerendering and verifies that the fallback remains cacheable.

This follows the reproduction, investigation, and proposed fix in #100841. We need to run deploy tests for this change. Those tests cannot run on fork PRs, so we are opening a branch PR in `vercel/next.js`.

Fixes #100829.
Closes #100841.

prs.title: turbopack: report chunk group consistency errors instead of panicking
prs.author: sokra
prs.body:
## Summary

Under eventual consistency, chunk group data from different graph versions can briefly be paired with each other. Two lookups still panic in that case. This PR makes both of them return errors, so the computation is retried once the data is consistent again.

- **Merged-parent lookups.** `ChunkGroupKey::ident_str` resolved the parent of an `IsolatedMerged`/`SharedMerged` key with `keys.index(parent)`. Some callers render a key whose parent index comes from another (e.g. newer) `ChunkGroupInfo` than `keys`, for example `ChunkGroupInfo::get_index_of`'s debug failure path and `chunk_group_content_operation`. That panicked with `chunk_group_info.rs: index out of bounds: the len is 28 but the index is 29` during `next build`.
  - The lookup is now checked and returns an error.
  - `keys` is narrowed to `&FxIndexSet<ChunkGroupKey>` (also for `debug_str`).
  - `ChunkGroup::debug_str` resolves parents through `chunk_group_at`.
  - The output of a successful render is unchanged, so asset names don't change.
- **`AvailableChunkGroups::assert_module_graph`.** This was a `debug_assert_eq!`. It now returns `Result`, and a graph mismatch is an error that names both graphs. The check is a cheap identity comparison, so it runs in all builds, not only debug builds.
  - `chunk_groups` and `with_chunk_group` now return `Result`, and callers propagate the error.
  - In `chunk_group_content_operation` the check runs once up front instead of in the per-module closures.

prs.title: Handle cancellation errors during response clone cleanup
prs.author: smaeda-ks
prs.body:
## Summary

A response body can fail after `fetch()` resolves, for example when an upstream connection closes. Even if the caller catches the body-read error, garbage-collection cleanup of an unused response clone can call `cancel()` on its already-errored stream.

That cancellation rejects, and the existing `.then(noop)` leaves the rejection unhandled. Depending on the runtime’s unhandled-rejection handling, this can terminate the process.

Use `.catch(noop)` to handle cancellation failures during cleanup. The original body-read error still reaches the caller.

Related: https://github.com/vrv/vercel-runtime-cache-cancel-repro

prs.title: Turbopack: use memchr3 for source position scanning and count astral chars as two UTF-16 columns
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

Turbopack's sectioned source maps compute each section's `offset` with `SourcePos::update`. It used to decode the generated code one UTF-8 character at a time. That loop was slow, and it counted a 4-byte (non-BMP) character such as `🦀` as one column even though source-map columns are UTF-16 code units, where it takes two. So any section that started after an astral character on the same line got an offset column that was too small.

`SourcePos::update` now works like the line index in `next-code-frame`'s highlighter:
- `memchr3` finds line-terminator candidates (`\n`, `\r`, and the `0xE2` lead byte of U+2028/U+2029). The JS terminator semantics are kept: `\r\n` counts as one terminator, and only `E2 80 A8` / `E2 80 A9` count as line/paragraph separators.
- Only the text after the last terminator affects the column, so only that segment is counted. A small `utf16_len(&[u8])` helper counts its UTF-16 units byte by byte: continuation bytes count 0, 4-byte lead bytes count 2, everything else counts 1. This is exact for UTF-8, safe on arbitrary bytes, and needs no `unsafe` or new dependency. A TODO points at switching to `simd-utf16-len` once it gains a byte-slice API (SyMind/simd-utf16-len#22).

`memchr` was already a workspace dependency; `turbopack-core` now uses it too.

`Code::generate_source_map_ref` calls `SourcePos::update` once per rope chunk, so its docs and `SourcePos::update`'s docs now state the contract this relies on: each chunk must be self-contained t

prs.title: turbopack: drop ASTs of tree-shaken modules
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
## Summary

Release parsed ASTs of tree-shaken modules during binding-usage analysis. Analysis retains ASTs for code generation to consume and release, but these modules never reach codegen.

Add `Vc::drop_content_hint()` to resolve a reference with normal output-dependency tracking, then drop the cell content without reading or recomputing missing content. Binding-usage analysis calls a default no-op `Module::drop_code_gen_data_hint()` for unused modules; ecmascript modules drop their parse result. Cleanup runs only for the whole-app graph and adds no extra tasks.

## Verification

- 1,283 Rust tests and 111 production tests pass on the AST-only change.
- Mixed fixture releases 43 resident ASTs; all 61 compared JS/HTML/CSS files match the baseline.

Independent companion: #100896 (Pages entry).

prs.title: Turbopack: resolve per-module data once during module graph construction
prs.author: lukesandberg
prs.body:
### Why

Several passes over the module graph need a per-module property: async module info, side-effect analysis, module merging, module ids, server actions, NFT, and build feature telemetry. Each one got it by calling a turbo-tasks function (`ident()`, `is_self_async()`, `side_effects()`, `is_mergeable()`, `ident().to_string()`) on every module in the graph.

Each of those calls adds a child edge from the pass's task to the module's task, so every pass ends by connecting tens of thousands of children, and those connects are expensive. On `canary`, `project_feature_usage` alone connects 92k children: 14.6s of CPU that occupies all 14 worker threads for 1.3s, just after all entrypoints are written.

### What

The module graph resolves these values once, while it is built, and stores them per graph. The passes read them from the graph instead of calling into every module.

- `ident` and `is_self_async` are always collected. `ident_string`, `side_effects` and `is_mergeable` are only collected when the pass that needs them runs, via new `ModuleGraphOptions` bits. A pass on a graph built without its bit fails rather than silently falling back to per-module calls.
- The values are resolved inline during graph construction, not in a task per module, and graph nodes stay the same size as on `canary`.

### Performance

Measured on a large internal app (`next build --experimental-build-mode=compile`, persistent cache on, release binaries) against the `canary` commit this is based on.
